usage: with prices Korean says 비싸다/싸다 (expensive/cheap), never 높다/낮다
object marker 을 + 물어보다 'ask and see'
깎다 'to shave/cut' is the verb for haggling
drop the particle in speech; 좀 softens the request
examples: 이거 가격이 얼마예요?
How much is the price of this?
simple: point at an item with 이거 and ask
이 옷은 가격이 너무 비싸요.
These clothes are way too expensive.
everyday: 너무 'too' + 비싸요, the default price adjective
가격은 좀 비싼데 품질이 좋아서 살게요.
The price is a bit high, but the quality is good so I'll buy it.
real situation: weighing 가격 against 품질 (quality) out loud
nuance: 가격(價格) is Sino-Korean — 價 'value/price' + 格 'standard' — so it literally means the 'value-standard' set on a thing, the official posted price. Its native-Korean twin is 값, and the line is feel and register: 값 is shorter, warmer, and used in fixed everyday phrases (값이 싸다, 값을 치르다), while 가격 sounds more neutral and 'tag/system' (가격표 price tag, 가격 인상 price hike) and is what you read on signs. The biggest English-speaker trap is the adjective: a high price is 비싸요 (expensive), a low price is 싸요 (cheap) — Koreans do NOT say 가격이 높아요/낮아요 the way English says 'high/low price', so importing 'high' here sounds off. Note too that to ask a clerk you rarely say the noun at all: the natural line is just 얼마예요? ('how much?'). 가격 collocates with 비싸다, 싸다, 오르다 (rise), 내리다 (drop), and 깎다 (haggle down).

mistakes: Saying 가격이 높아요 for 'the price is high' — that is a direct translation of English; Korean uses 비싸요 (expensive). Use 높다/낮다 only for height or numbers like temperature, not for prices.
Treating 가격 and 값 as freely swappable — they overlap, but you say 값을 치르다 (pay the price), not 가격을 치르다, and 가격표 (price tag), not 값표. Learn them as set phrases.
Asking a shopkeeper 가격이 뭐예요? ('what is the price?'). The natural question is 얼마예요? or 가격이 얼마예요?, never 뭐예요 for an amount.

usage: 할인 + 되다 'gets done'; the price-side passive, 'it is discounted'
받다 'receive' — you, the customer, are the receiver
할인하다 + 주다; what you actually say to bargain
-(으)ㄹ 수 있다 'be able to' for asking if it's possible
examples: 오늘 이거 할인돼요?
Is this discounted today?
simple: 할인되다 as one verb, 'get discounted'
학생은 할인을 받을 수 있어요?
Can students get a discount?
everyday: 받다 puts the customer as receiver of the discount
회원이면 10퍼센트 할인해 드릴게요.
If you're a member, I'll give you 10 percent off.
real situation: a clerk speaking up, using 해 드리다 (humble 'do for you')
nuance: 할인(割引) is Sino-Korean — 割 'cut' + 引 'pull (down)' — literally 'cut and pull down', i.e. knock money off a price. The key contrast for learners is 할인 vs 세일: 할인 is the abstract act/amount of reducing a price on an item ('10% off', a discount), while 세일 (from English 'sale') names a store-wide selling event (백화점 세일 a department-store sale). So a 세일 contains many 할인s. Watch the voice carefully: from the price's point of view you say 할인이 되다/할인되다 ('it gets discounted'); from your point of view as buyer you say 할인을 받다 ('I receive a discount'); and to actively ask for one you say 할인해 주세요 ('please discount it for me'). The English-speaker pitfall is firing 할인해요 at a clerk hoping it means 'give me a discount' — bare 할인해요 just states 'someone discounts', so it lands as a flat description, not a request. Add 주세요/돼요 to make it work. Common partners: 할인되다, 할인받다, 할인 행사 (discount event), 할인 쿠폰.

Mixing up the receiver: customers say 할인을 받다 (receive a discount), shops say 할인을 해 주다 (give a discount). Saying 할인을 줘요 about yourself ('I give a discount') reverses the roles.
Using 세일 when you mean a discount on one item. 'This bag is 30% off' is 이 가방은 30퍼센트 할인이에요, not 세일이에요 — 세일 is the whole event, not the single markdown.

usage: (으)로 'by means of' is THE particle for payment method
현금 영수증 is the tax receipt clerks ask about
examples: 저는 현금으로 낼게요.
I'll pay with cash.
simple: 으로 marks the method, 낼게요 'I'll pay' shows your intention
지금 현금이 좀 모자라요.
I'm a bit short on cash right now.
everyday: 모자라다 'be short/lacking' is more natural here than 없다
여기는 카드 안 되고 현금만 받아요.
They don't take card here, only cash.
real situation: contrasting 카드 vs 현금 with 만 'only'
nuance: 현금(現金) is Sino-Korean — 現 'present/actual' + 金 'gold/money' — literally 'actual money', i.e. physical notes and coins you hand over, as opposed to 카드 (card) or 계좌이체 (bank transfer). The crucial grammar point is the particle: payment method takes 으로/로 ('by means of'), so 'pay with cash' is 현금으로 내다/계산하다 — English speakers reach for 'with' and wrongly grab 와/하고 (which mean 'together with a person/thing') or 에 (location/time). 현금 is more specific than the umbrella word 돈 (money): 돈 covers wealth in general, but 현금 specifically means money in hand right now (you can have lots of 돈 in the bank but no 현금 in your wallet). A very useful real-life phrase is 현금 영수증 ('cash receipt') — a registered receipt for tax deduction that clerks routinely offer with 현금 영수증 해 드릴까요? Collocations: 현금으로 내다/계산하다/결제하다, 현금만 받다, 현금이 모자라다.

mistakes: Using 에 or 하고 for 'with cash' — 현금에 내요 or 현금하고 내요 are wrong. The means particle is 으로: 현금으로 내요. Reserve 하고/와 for accompaniment ('with a friend').
Treating 현금 and 돈 as identical. 돈이 없어요 can mean you're broke overall; 현금이 없어요 specifically means you have no physical cash on you (maybe you have a card). Pick the one you mean.
Forgetting that 되다 marks acceptability: 'is cash OK?' is 현금 돼요?, and 'cash only' is 현금만 돼요. Saying 현금 있어요? to ask a shop's policy asks whether the SHOP has cash, not whether they accept it.

usage: 있다 'exist/have'; subject 이 because 동전 ends in a consonant
(으)로 again marks the means of payment
개 is the counter for small objects: 동전 한 개, 두 개
examples: 지갑에 동전이 많아요.
I have a lot of coins in my wallet.
simple: 에 marks location (in the wallet), 많아요 'are many'
동전 다섯 개로 자판기에서 음료를 샀어요.
I bought a drink from the vending machine with five coins.
everyday: counter 개 + 으로 for paying with coins
주머니에 동전이 가득해서 걸을 때마다 짤랑거려요.
My pocket is full of coins, so they jingle every time I walk.
real situation: 가득하다 'be full' + the onomatopoeia 짤랑거리다 'jingle'
nuance: 동전(銅錢) is Sino-Korean — 銅 'copper' + 錢 'coin/money' — literally 'copper money', the metal money minted as coins (10원, 100원, 500원). Its partner is 지폐(紙幣) 'paper currency' = bills; together 동전 + 지폐 make up 현금. So the dividing line is material: 동전 = metal coins, 지폐 = paper notes, and you must not call a 1,000원 note a 동전. A second word to keep separate is 잔돈, which means 'small change / leftover change' — 잔돈 is about the FUNCTION (the change you get back), and can be coins or small bills, whereas 동전 strictly names the coin object. The English-speaker pitfall is also the counter: coins are counted with 개 (동전 세 개 'three coins'), not with a 'piece' word you might invent, and the means particle for paying is 으로 (동전으로). Collocations: 동전을 모으다 (collect coins), 동전을 바꾸다 (break a bill into coins), 동전이 무겁다, 동전 지갑 (coin purse).

Confusing 동전 with 잔돈. When you want 'keep the change', say 잔돈은 괜찮아요, not 동전은 괜찮아요 — 잔돈 is the change you receive, which may include small bills, while 동전 just names coins as objects.

usage: 있다 'have'; 이 because it ends in a consonant
두고 오다 'put down and came' — the set phrase for forgetting things
I take a card out of the wallet
examples: 제 지갑이 가방 안에 있어요.
My wallet is inside my bag.
simple: 안에 'inside' locates 지갑 within 가방
지갑을 집에 두고 와서 돈이 하나도 없어요.
I left my wallet at home, so I have no money at all.
everyday: 두고 오다 for forgetting + 하나도 없다 'not even one'
지하철에서 누가 제 지갑을 훔쳐 갔어요.
Someone stole my wallet on the subway.
real situation: 훔쳐 가다 'steal and take away', a phrase you'd need in an emergency
nuance: 지갑(紙匣) is Sino-Korean — 紙 'paper' + 匣 'small box/case' — historically a 'paper case', now the small folding holder for your money, cards, and ID. Don't confuse it with 가방, which is the larger bag/handbag/backpack you carry items in: a 지갑 typically goes INSIDE a 가방. Modern usage has stretched 지갑 to digital things too — your phone's payment app is a 모바일 지갑 ('mobile wallet') — but the core image is the physical billfold. A subtle pitfall is the verb of forgetting: English 'I forgot my wallet' becomes Korean 지갑을 두고 왔어요 ('I put it down and came'), NOT 지갑을 잊어버렸어요 — 잊어버리다 is for forgetting information/facts (a name, an appointment), while physically leaving an object behind is 두고 오다. For losing it irretrievably you use 잃어버리다. Collocations: 지갑을 열다 (open the wallet → spend), 지갑이 가볍다/두둑하다 (thin/fat wallet = broke/flush), 지갑을 챙기다 (grab your wallet), 동전 지갑 (coin purse).

Forgetting the particle when taking something out: it's 지갑에서 카드를 꺼내다 (out of the wallet), using 에서 for the source, not 지갑에 (which would mark a destination or static location).

usage: 주다 'give' + 세요; the standard checkout request
필요하다 'be needed'; the thing needed takes 가/이
please put it in a bag
plastic bags are paid (봉투 값), a real-life detail in Korea
examples: 봉투 하나 주세요.
Please give me one bag.
simple: drop the particle in speech, 하나 'one' as a loose counter
따로따로 봉투에 넣어 주세요.
Please put them in separate bags.
everyday: 따로따로 'separately' + 에 넣다, a real checkout request
봉투는 100원인데 필요하세요?
The bag costs 100 won — do you need one?
real situation: a clerk asking, since paid bags are law in Korea
nuance: 봉투(封套) is Sino-Korean — 封 'seal/close' + 套 'cover/case' — literally a 'sealing cover', i.e. a flat sleeve. That's why one word covers two things: the thin shopping bag a shop gives you (비닐봉투 plastic, 종이봉투 paper) AND a paper envelope for letters or money (편지봉투 letter envelope, and the cash gift envelopes used at weddings/funerals). Contrast it sharply with 가방, the sturdy bag with handles you own and reuse (backpack, handbag, suitcase): a 봉투 is flimsy and disposable, a 가방 is a possession. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'bag' maps onto BOTH, so learners say 봉투 when they mean a backpack — wrong; that's 가방/배낭. A useful cultural-practical note: in Korea store bags are not free, so 봉투 값 ('bag fee') and the clerk's question 봉투 드릴까요? / 봉투 필요하세요? are everyday phrases worth knowing. Collocations: 봉투에 넣다 (put in a bag), 봉투를 주다/받다, 비닐봉투, 종이봉투, 봉투 값.

examples: 계산대가 어디예요?
Where is the checkout counter?
simple: basic location question with 어디
저쪽 계산대에서 계산하시면 돼요.
You can pay at that checkout over there.
everyday: 저쪽 'that way' + 에서 + -시면 돼요 'you may/just'
계산대마다 줄이 너무 길어서 셀프 계산대로 갔어요.
Every checkout had such a long line that I went to the self-checkout.
real situation: 마다 'each' + 셀프 계산대 (self-checkout), a modern store reality
nuance: 계산대(計算臺) is Sino-Korean — 計算 'calculation/reckoning' + 臺 'platform/stand' — literally the 'reckoning platform', the counter where the total is tallied and you pay. Keep three related words apart: 계산대 is the PLACE (the physical counter), 계산 is the ACT of paying/settling up (계산할게요 'I'll pay'), and 계산서 is the BILL/check that lists what you owe (common in restaurants). So you walk 계산대로 (to the counter), do the 계산 (paying), and may read a 계산서 (bill). The two direction-vs-location particles matter: heading toward it is 계산대로 가다 (으)로 for direction), but the paying happens 계산대에서 (에서 for the location of an action). The English-speaker pitfall is using 계산대 as if it were the action — 'I'll do the checkout' is 계산할게요 (verb 계산하다), not 계산대 할게요. In modern stores you'll also meet 셀프 계산대 (self-checkout) and 무인 계산대 (unmanned kiosk). Collocations: 계산대로 가다, 계산대에서 계산하다, 계산대 줄, 셀프 계산대.

계산대(計算臺) is Sino-Korean — 計算 'calculation/reckoning' + 臺 'platform/stand' — literally the 'reckoning platform'.

The two direction-vs-location particles matter: heading toward it is 계산대로 가다 (으)로 for direction), but the paying happens 계산대에서 (에서 for the location of an action). The English-speaker pitfall is using 계산대 as if it were the action — 'I'll do the checkout' is 계산할게요 (verb 계산하다), not 계산대 할게요.

mistakes: Confusing 계산대 (the counter, a place) with 계산 (the act of paying). 'I'll pay' is 계산할게요, not 계산대 할게요. The -대 ending names the physical stand.
Mixing the particles: go 계산대로 (toward it, direction 로), but pay 계산대에서 (at it, action location 에서). Saying 계산대에 계산해요 misuses 에 for an action that needs 에서.
Saying 계산서 when you mean the counter. 계산서 is the itemized bill/check (mostly at restaurants); the counter you pay at is 계산대.

usage: 많다 'be many'; subject 이 after a consonant
분 is the honorific counter for people, raising respect
모시다 is the humble verb for serving a respected person
examples: 오늘 가게에 손님이 많아요.
There are a lot of customers in the shop today.
simple: 에 marks the location, 많아요 'are many'
손님 한 분이 입구에서 기다리고 계세요.
One customer is waiting at the entrance.
everyday: honorific 분 + 계시다 to respectfully describe the customer
손님, 이쪽으로 오시겠어요?
Sir/Ma'am, would you come this way?
real situation: 손님 used as a direct address term by staff, with honorific -시-
nuance: 손님 is native Korean — 손 'guest' + the honorific suffix -님 — so it builds 'guest' into a respectful form, and it covers BOTH a paying customer in a shop AND a guest visiting your home. That built-in 님 is why 손님 is inherently polite and why staff address you directly as 손님 (like English 'sir/ma'am'). Contrast it with the neutral 사람 'person' (too plain and even rude to call a customer) and with 고객, the more formal/corporate term banks, telecoms, and notices use (고객님, 고객 센터 customer center) — 손님 feels face-to-face and shop-floor, 고객 feels institutional. Because 손님 deserves respect, it's counted with the honorific 분 (손님 한 분, not 한 명) and described with honorific verbs (오시다 'come', 계시다 'be present', 기다리고 계세요). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 사람 ('a person came to the shop' → 사람이 왔어요 sounds cold); say 손님이 오셨어요. Collocations: 손님을 받다 (take/receive customers), 손님이 들다 (customers come in), 단골손님 (regular), 손님 접대 (hosting guests).

usage: 친절하다 'be kind/courteous', a typical thing to say about staff
부르다 'call'; in real life you'd say 저기요 to get attention
examples: 이 가게 점원이 아주 친절해요.
The clerk at this shop is very kind.
simple: describing staff with 친절하다
점원에게 다른 색깔이 있는지 물어봤어요.
I asked the clerk if there was another color.
everyday: 에게 (to the clerk) + -는지 'whether' embedded question
저기요, 이거 입어 봐도 돼요?
Excuse me, can I try this on?
real situation: in practice you call out 저기요 to a clerk, not 점원!
nuance: 점원(店員) is Sino-Korean — 店 'shop/store' + 員 'member/staff' — literally a 'shop staff member', the salesperson who works the floor and helps customers, the natural counterpart to 손님 (customer). Distinguish nearby words: 직원(職員) is the broader 'employee/staff' of any organization (office, bank, company), while 점원 specifically means a shop assistant; 사장(님) is the boss/owner; and 알바(생) is a part-timer. The single most important pitfall for English speakers is that 점원 is a descriptive label, not an address term — you never call out '점원!' to summon them the way English barks 'Clerk!'. To get a clerk's attention you say 저기요 ('excuse me') or 여기요, and to refer to them respectfully you can say 직원분 or 사장님. So 점원 mostly appears when you TALK ABOUT staff (점원이 친절했어요), and you switch to 저기요 when you TALK TO them. The person to ask takes 에게/한테 (점원에게 물어보다). Collocations: 점원이 친절하다, 점원에게 묻다/물어보다, 점원이 도와주다, 점원을 부르다.

usage: 세일 + 하다; the store 'does' a sale
중 'in the middle of' = currently running
기간 'period/duration' + 세일, e.g. 세일 기간에 'during the sale'
examples: 지금 세일 중이에요?
Is there a sale on right now?
simple: 중이에요 'is in progress', a quick question to a clerk
이번 주에 백화점이 세일을 해요.
The department store is having a sale this week.
everyday: 세일을 하다 'hold a sale', the store as the doer
세일 기간이라 평소보다 훨씬 싸게 샀어요.
Since it was the sale period, I bought it much cheaper than usual.
real situation: 기간이라 '(because) it's the period' + 싸게 사다 'buy cheaply'
nuance: 세일 is a loanword from English 'sale', but Korean has narrowed it to mean specifically a store-wide markdown EVENT — a period when a whole shop or department store cuts prices (백화점 세일, 시즌 오프 세일). It is not the general word for 'selling': 'to sell' is the native verb 팔다, and a one-item price cut is 할인 (discount). So the sharp contrast is 세일 (the event/season) vs 할인 (the act/amount of discounting a given item): a bag inside a 세일 might have a 30% 할인. Grammatically 세일 pairs with 하다 (세일을 하다 'hold a sale') and lives in time phrases (세일 중, 세일 기간, 세일 때). The English-speaker pitfall is double: (1) don't use 세일 to mean 'sell' — 'I sold my phone' is 폰을 팔았어요, never 세일했어요; and (2) for a discount on a single product prefer 할인. Note also Korean keeps the borrowed -ㄹ sound, so it's 세일 (se-il), two syllables. Collocations: 세일을 하다, 세일 중이다, 세일 기간/때, 시즌 오프 세일.

Forgetting 세일 takes 하다 and time words. 'There's a sale now' is 지금 세일 중이에요 / 지금 세일해요, not 세일이에요 alone, which sounds incomplete.

usage: 받다 'receive'; you, the buyer, get your money back
환불하다 + 주세요; what you say to request it
환불 + 되다 'be doable', about store policy
-(으)ㄹ 수 있다 to ask if it's allowed
examples: 이거 환불돼요?
Can I get a refund on this?
simple: 환불되다 as one verb to ask about policy
영수증이 있으면 환불 받을 수 있어요.
If you have the receipt, you can get a refund.
everyday: -(으)면 'if' condition + 받을 수 있다 'can receive'
사이즈가 안 맞아서 환불하러 왔는데요, 카드로 결제했어요.
I came to get a refund because the size doesn't fit; I paid by card.
real situation: -러 오다 'come in order to' + explaining 결제 (payment) method
nuance: 환불(還拂) is Sino-Korean — 還 'return/give back' + 拂 'pay out' — literally 'pay back', i.e. returning the buyer's money for a returned item. The contrast learners must nail is 환불 vs 교환: 환불 = money back, 교환(交換 'exchange') = swap for a different item/size/color, no money returned. A related word is 반품(返品) 'returning the goods' — the physical act of sending the product back, which usually triggers a 환불. So you 반품 the item and receive a 환불. Voice matters as with 할인: from your side you say 환불을 받다 ('receive a refund'); to request it you say 환불해 주세요 ('refund it for me'); about whether it's allowed you say 환불이 되다/환불되다 ('a refund is possible'). The English-speaker pitfall is wanting an exchange but saying 환불 — if you actually want a different size, ask 교환돼요? / 교환해 주세요, because 환불 will give you cash back, not a swap. Note Korean also uses 결제 (결제하다) for 'make a payment/settle by card', often in the same conversation. Collocations: 환불을 받다, 환불해 주다, 환불되다, 환불 정책 (refund policy), 환불 규정.

usage: 주다 + 세요; the basic checkout request
필요하다 'be needed'; the needed thing takes 가/이
버리다 'throw away', a common follow-up action
examples: 영수증 좀 주세요.
Could I have the receipt, please?
simple: 좀 softens the request, particle dropped in speech
환불하려면 영수증이 꼭 필요해요.
You absolutely need the receipt to get a refund.
everyday: -려면 'if you want to' + 꼭 'definitely' tying 영수증 to 환불
영수증 드릴까요? 아니면 버려 드릴까요?
Would you like the receipt, or shall I throw it away for you?
real situation: the exact clerk's question, with humble 드리다 'give'
nuance: 영수증(領收證) is Sino-Korean — 領 'receive' + 收 'collect' + 證 'proof/certificate' — literally a 'proof of receiving (payment)', the printed slip showing the shop got your money. Distinguish it from 계산서(計算書) 'the bill/check', which is the itemized statement of what you OWE (you read a 계산서 before paying, mostly at restaurants), whereas the 영수증 is issued AFTER you pay as proof. Also keep 영수증 apart from 현금 영수증, a specifically Korean tax-deduction receipt tied to your phone number that clerks ask about separately. Because clerks routinely offer it, you'll constantly hear the polite 영수증 드릴까요? ('shall I give you the receipt?', humble 드리다 raising you the customer), and the practical answer is 네, 주세요 or 아니요, 괜찮아요.
